Standpoint Epistemology
STAND-point ih-pis-tuh-MOL-uh-jee
noun phrase
Academic coinage of the 1970s-80s feminist academy — Nancy Hartsock's "feminist standpoint" (1983), systematized by Sandra Harding — adapting the Marxist claim that the proletariat sees class reality more truly than its masters. Standpoint (where one stands) + epistemology (theory of knowledge): the theory that knowledge is determined by social position.

📖 Biblical Definition

The claim that truth is indexed to social location — that the marginalized possess privileged access to knowledge by virtue of their oppression, so that "lived experience" outranks argument, evidence, and testimony from outside the favored group. Scripture flatly contradicts both halves. First, truth is grounded in God, not in position: his word is truth (John 17:17), and it addresses kings and beggars on identical terms. Second, Scripture forbids epistemic partiality in BOTH directions: "thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour" (Lev. 19:15) — a verse that anticipates and condemns the standpoint move by name, since tilting the scales toward the poor man's testimony is the form of partiality the modern academy baptizes. Experience is real data, but it arrives through a heart that is "deceitful above all things" (Jer. 17:9) and must be weighed: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Prov. 18:17). Every claim — from any standpoint — faces the same court: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thes. 5:21).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

No Webster 1828 entry — the phrase is a late-20th-century academic coinage. Webster would have filed the underlying questions under KNOWLEDGE and TESTIMONY, both of which his definitions ground in evidence rather than in the witness's social station.

expand to see more

STANDPOINT EPISTEMOLOGY, noun phrase. Feminist-Marxist theory of knowledge: Hartsock's 'The Feminist Standpoint' (1983), Harding's 'strong objectivity' (1991) — knowledge is socially situated; marginalized positions yield epistemic privilege.

The pipeline runs Marx (class consciousness) → feminist standpoint theory → critical race theory's 'unique voice of color' → the popular idiom 'listen to lived experience.'

In practice it functions as an unanswerable-argument machine: disagreement from outside the favored standpoint is reclassified as evidence of the speaker's blindness, so the thesis can never be falsified — the mark of ideology rather than knowledge.

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 19:15 — "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour."

Proverbs 18:17 — "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him."

Jeremiah 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

2 Corinthians 13:1 — "This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established."

1 Thessalonians 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

John 7:24 — "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Not itself a corrupted word but a corrupting framework — it relocates the ground of truth from God's revelation to group identity, and it has leaked from the seminar room into the church.

expand to see more

The framework entered evangelical spaces wearing pastoral clothes: "we need to listen to marginalized voices" — which, as a call to hear testimony and examine it, is simply Proverbs 18:17. But standpoint epistemology smuggles in a second clause: that the testimony may not be searched, because searching it is itself oppression. At that point listening has been converted from the beginning of judgment into the end of it, and Lev. 19:15's forbidden partiality has been rebranded as righteousness.

The practical fruit in the church: staff trainings where disagreement is recoded as 'fragility,' testimonies that function as trump cards, and shepherds afraid to weigh an accusation because the accuser holds the favored standpoint. Scripture's witness-law is the antidote — two or three witnesses (2 Cor. 13:1), cross-examination (Prov. 18:17), no respect of persons in either direction (Lev. 19:15) — a jurisprudence that protects the genuinely oppressed far better than epistemic privilege does, because it cannot be captured by whoever shouts their standing loudest.

The deepest error is theological: standpoint epistemology is a doctrine of revelation with the Revealer deleted. It correctly senses that fallen man's knowing is corrupted and partial — total depravity reaches the mind — but instead of looking up to the God whose word cuts through every situated heart, it crowns one class of situated hearts as the oracle. The Reformed answer is not that the comfortable see clearly, but that NO flesh sees clearly, "but God" (Eph. 2:4) speaks — and his word judges every standpoint, including the marginal one.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Marxist class-consciousness, retooled by the feminist academy (Hartsock 1983, Harding 1991), flowing into CRT's 'voice of color' and the street idiom 'lived experience.'

expand to see more

Marx/Lukács: the proletariat's position grants truer sight of class reality — the template for all standpoint claims.

Hartsock 1983: 'The Feminist Standpoint' — women's social position yields epistemic privilege about gendered reality.

Harding 1991: 'strong objectivity' — research should START from marginalized lives; neutrality is recast as bias.

CRT adoption: the 'unique voice of color' thesis — see [[critical-race-theory]] — and from there the popular commandment to 'center lived experience.'

Biblical counter-grammar: mishpat (H4941, judgment) bound to witnesses and evidence; prosopolepsia (G4382, respect of persons) condemned in James 2:1-9 — partiality is sin regardless of which face is favored.

Usage

"The moment a claim cannot be questioned without the questioner being indicted, you are no longer dealing with testimony — that is standpoint epistemology doing its work."

"Lev. 19:15 forbids tilting the scale toward the mighty AND toward the poor; standpoint epistemology calls the second tilt justice, and Moses calls it unrighteousness."

"She said her lived experience settled the matter; the elder gently answered that experience is a witness to be heard and weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed."
